posts.text:
Some random thoughts about Jensen.

Jensen met his wife Lori when he was just 17, got married, had kids, and started Nvidia at 30.

He then spent the next 33 years working his ass off building Nvidia into one of the most important companies in the world.

I imagine he probably missed out on a lot of things most young people experience, especially dating and relationships.

I think it’s just human nature. When you’re young and don’t get to experience certain things, you may feel like you’re missing out. And sometimes that feeling stays with you for the rest of your life.

Even when you’re 60, with all the money and success in the world, you may still want to experience what you missed in your 20s.

Maybe that’s part of what happened to Jensen. I don’t know.

I’m not trying to justify what he did. He was incredibly reckless, and it cost him something he spent more than half his life building.

But I also think we sometimes forget that Jensen is just a human being, with desires and weaknesses like the rest of us.

Maybe he spent so much of his life building Nvidia that somewhere along the way, he wanted to experience the life he never really had.

The saddest part for me is how quickly he was pushed out of the very company he built from scratch.

This is a man who literally has the Nvidia logo tattooed on his body, who has called Nvidia his life’s work, working every waking hour, and who dedicated more than half his life to it.

NVIDIA employees: go on strike. Now.

Not for a raise. Not for more PTO. For your founder.

Jensen Huang was just pushed out in four days, after thirty-three years building the company. The GPU, CUDA, the entire infrastructure the world's AI runs on today. And it ends with a three-line press release on a Thursday morning.

Here are the facts. Sunday, Huang admits to an affair and apologizes to his teams. The board launches an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton and a former federal prosecutor. Thursday, he resigns under pressure. The investigation hasn't reached any conclusion. No technology leak has been established. No misconduct has been announced.

The sentence came before the verdict.

And it has worked before.

November 2023. OpenAI's board fires Sam Altman on a Friday night. Within days, more than 700 of roughly 770 employees sign a letter: bring Altman back, or we all walk. Five days later, Altman is back, and most of the board that fired him is gone.

Call it the Altman precedent: in a company built on talent, real power doesn't sit with the board. It sits with the people who build.

I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at http://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

I think it’s time to revisit the accredited investor laws in the US.

Companies are staying private longer, where only accredited investors (aka rich people!) can invest. Retail investors can only come in after IPO, when much of the upside has already been captured.

These rules were created with the best of intentions, to protect regular people from scams - a noble idea. Unfortunately, in practice they've often made it illegal to get richer, unless you're already rich. A regressive tax!

We have to judge policies based on their outcomes, not on their intentions.

These are two possible routes I see:

1) Replace the rule with something merit-based, like a financial literacy test. Pass it and you're accredited. Having a qualification based on competency rather than your bank balance or income seems far more fair.

2) Remove the rule entirely. Let consenting adults assess their own risk. Disclosure requirements stay and fraud enforcement stays to punish bad actors.

posts.name: Raoul Pal
posts.text:
GDP only grows three ways... more people, more debt or more productivity. 

More people is gone. Demographics were set in stone 30 years ago and nobody can change them. The workforce is shrinking and ageing, so the growth that used to come from simply adding workers has been fading for two decades.

For the last 15 years the gap left by people has been filled with borrowing, more and more of it, until we're now borrowing to pay the interest on the borrowing. That's the debasement everyone feels but cant name. And that lever is spent too.

Which leaves the third one. Productivity. But here's the problem... productivity has always meant people producing more, and we are running out of people. The only way to get a step change in output with fewer workers is machines.

AI and robotics are not a nice to have. They are the one lever still available, and they are the only thing that can get us out of this mess and outgrow the debt rather than inflate it away.

So yes, people are worried about the robots taking their jobs. The alternative is a system with no way out.

What does change is who the value flows to. It goes to whoever owns the networks...

So if the robots are coming for our jobs, then we had bloody well better own the robots.
